title: Signature MPC Audit Trail
description: Signature edition: every MPC session journals its transcript commitments — protocol, parties, input commitments, output — so the computation's integrity is auditable without revealing inputs. Disputes resolve against the transcript, not against anyone's word. This is a Signature original method.
method: Commit to inputs; journal the transcript; verify commitments match the output; the trail resolves disputes.
usage: Journal all production MPC sessions; use the trail for dispute resolution.

demo.code:
print('session #441: 3 parties, protocol SPDZ, input commitments c1..c3')
print('output verified against commitments -> AUDITED')

title: Signature Garbled circuits (Yao)
description: Signature edition: Yao's garbled circuits let two parties compute a function on private inputs: one garbles the circuit (encrypting truth tables), the other evaluates it obliviously via oblivious transfer. Neither learns the other's input beyond the output — secure two-party computation from symmetric crypto.
method: Garbler encrypts gates; evaluator obtains input labels via OT; evaluates gate by gate; decodes only the output labels.
usage: Use for two-party functions (auctions, matching); the circuit must be known to both.

demo.code:
print('garbled AND gate: 4 encrypted rows')
print('evaluator with labels (1,0) decrypts exactly one row -> output 0')
print('neither party learns the other\'s input bit')

title: Signature Threshold cryptography
description: Signature edition: Threshold signatures and decryption split a key across n parties; any t can sign/decrypt, fewer cannot. It's MPC for a single operation — protecting CA keys, crypto wallets, and root credentials so no single party (or thief) holds the key.
method: Distributed key generation; t parties collaborate per operation; the full key never exists in one place.
usage: Protect high-value keys with threshold schemes; choose t for your availability/security tradeoff.

demo.code:
print('3-of-5 threshold signature: parties 1,3,4 collaborate')
print('valid signature produced; full key never existed anywhere')

title: Signature Oblivious transfer
description: Signature edition: Oblivious transfer is MPC's core primitive: the sender has two messages, the receiver picks one, the sender doesn't learn which, the receiver learns nothing about the other. OT extension (IKNP) amortizes base OTs into millions cheaply — nearly all practical MPC runs on OT extension.
method: Base OTs via public-key crypto; extend to millions with symmetric crypto (IKNP); build garbled circuits and GMW on top.
usage: Use OT extension libraries; never implement base OT yourself.

demo.code:
print('sender: [m0, m1]; receiver choice: 1')
print('receiver learns m1 only; sender learns nothing about the choice')

title: Signature MP-SPDZ framework
description: Signature edition: MP-SPDZ implements 30+ MPC protocols behind one Python-like frontend: write the computation once, run it under semi-honest, malicious, honest/dishonest majority protocols. It's the compiler that made MPC experimentally accessible — protocol choice becomes a flag, not a rewrite.
method: Write in the MP-SPDZ DSL; compile; select the protocol backend; run across parties.
usage: Prototype in MP-SPDZ; benchmark protocol backends for your function; deploy the winner.

demo.code:
print('program: sfix average of private inputs')
print('run: -b semi-honest (fast) vs -b malicious (safe) — same program')

title: Signature MPC for private ML inference
description: Signature edition: Two or three servers jointly evaluate a neural network on a client's private input: the client secret-shares its data, servers compute under MPC, and only the client learns the result. Private inference without trusting any single server — deployed for medical and financial models.
method: Secret-share the input; evaluate the network layer by layer under MPC; return shares of the output to the client.
usage: Use for high-value private inference; quantize models to reduce MPC cost.

demo.code:
print('client shares x-ray; 3 servers evaluate tumor-model under MPC')
print('client reconstructs: diagnosis; servers learned nothing')

title: Signature SPDZ (malicious majority)
description: Signature edition: SPDZ handles the hard case: malicious parties in dishonest majority, using somewhat-homomorphic encryption for a preprocessing phase that generates authenticated multiplication triples. Online phase is fast information-theoretic MPC with MACs catching cheaters — abort on misbehavior.
method: Preprocess: generate Beaver triples with MACs; online: consume triples for multiplications; verify MACs; abort on failure.
usage: Use when parties don't trust each other; the offline phase can run before inputs are known.

demo.code:
print('offline: 1M triples generated (SHE)')
print('online: multiplication = 2 opens + MAC check -> cheater caught, abort')

title: Signature GMW protocol
description: Signature edition: Goldreich-Micali-Wigderson extends secure computation to many parties with boolean circuits and OT: each party holds XOR-shares of every wire, and gates are evaluated interactively. GMW is the multi-party workhorse — conceptually simple, secure against semi-honest majorities.
method: Share inputs as XOR shares; evaluate AND gates via OT, XOR gates locally; reconstruct only the final output.
usage: Use for multi-party boolean computations; budget the OT rounds (they dominate cost).

demo.code:
print('3 parties, XOR-shared inputs')
print('AND gate: 1 OT round -> shares of output; XOR gates: free')

title: Signature BGW protocol
description: Signature edition: Ben-Or, Goldwasser, Wigderson brought MPC to arithmetic circuits with Shamir shares: additions are local, multiplications need one interaction round (degree reduction). BGW tolerates t < n/3 malicious parties — information-theoretic security, no crypto assumptions at all.
method: Shamir-share inputs; add locally; multiply with degree-reduction interaction; reconstruct the output.
usage: Use for arithmetic MPC (statistics, ML) with honest-majority assumptions.

demo.code:
print('shares of a, b; c = a*b via degree reduction (1 round)')
print('output reconstructed; no party saw a or b')
